model_visible.headline: From Training to Production, NVIDIA and CoreWeave Close the Loop on Agentic AI
model_visible.excerpt: NVIDIA says CoreWeave is bringing the Vera Rubin generation into production on its AI cloud. At CoreWeave Fully Connected, CoreWeave announced availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems with Spectrum-X 102.4T Ethernet networking. Cognition, the company behind the Devin software engineer, is identified as the first customer running production workloads on Vera Rubin. NVIDIA also says CoreWeave will offer Vera, a CPU designed for AI-agent workloads. The article frames the move as continuity across multiple generations of NVIDIA compute, networking, and software rather than a one-off accelerator swap. For the Brief, the verified mechanism is production infrastructure for agentic workloads, not an independent claim that the platform improves every agent workload.

model_visible.headline: Add Runtime Controls to AI Agents with NVIDIA OpenShell
model_visible.excerpt: NVIDIA describes OpenShell 0.1.0 as an open-source runtime that adds enforceable controls around existing AI agents without requiring teams to rewrite the agent. The runtime combines sandboxed execution, controlled service access, credential management, network policy, and formal policy analysis. Its example shows read-only GitHub access being allowed while write requests are blocked, with policy decisions visible in logs. Credentials can remain outside the agent workload and be substituted only for approved destinations. Policy changes can require human review, and the policy prover checks modeled permissions independently of the agent’s own explanation. The verified lesson is that runtime enforcement can sit outside a long-running agent and constrain what it can actually do.

model_visible.headline: Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents
model_visible.excerpt: The Hugging Face team article presents ProvenanceGuard, a post-generation verifier for MCP-based agents that preserves source identity instead of pooling all tool evidence together. The system decomposes an answer into claims, routes each claim to a likely source, checks whether that source supports it, compares that source with the one named or implied by the answer, and produces claim-level plus overall allow/block decisions. The authors focus on cross-source conflation: a claim may be true somewhere in the evidence but wrongly attributed to another tool output. In reported medical-agent tests, the approach caught nearly all expert-labeled claims that should be blocked, while also sending some supported claims for review. The article explicitly notes remaining source-identification limits.

model_visible.headline: Helping small businesses put AI to work
model_visible.excerpt: OpenAI announced a partnership with America’s SBDC to expand hands-on AI training and local guidance for small businesses. The initial plan is to train about 150 Small Business Development Center advisors and reach at least 1,000 businesses through workshops, advising, and reusable resources. OpenAI also published a report saying roughly four million employees at firms with fewer than 500 people used OpenAI tools during a recent September week. The report describes small-business use in finance, supply chain, legal and compliance, marketing, competitive pricing, research, and outreach. The practical signal is not merely tool access: OpenAI is pairing workflow examples with local advisors who can help owners choose a starting task, test it, and assess whether it helps.

model_visible.headline: How Anthropic's sales team rebuilt inbound with Claude Managed Agents
model_visible.excerpt: Anthropic describes an internal buying agent built on Claude Managed Agents to handle inbound sales questions and guide prospects toward purchase or human handoff. The company says the agent now handles thousands of conversations per day and can answer questions about pricing, security, data, plans, and seat counts. Conversations end in purchase, a handoff with context for a sales representative, or a quick answer. Anthropic reports that escalated customers become sales opportunities more than twice as often as leads from the former form and close about five days faster. The article also describes treating escalation reasons as feedback for improving the experience. These are publisher-reported operational results, not an independent comparative study.

model_visible.headline: Claude for Government is now generally available
model_visible.excerpt: Anthropic announced general availability of Claude for Government for federal and state agencies in a FedRAMP High authorized environment. The product lets agency staff work directly with desktop files and use skills, plugins, and projects for tasks such as memo creation, RFP review, and casework. The company says administrators can set configuration defaults, allocate and control spending across departments, connect identity providers, and review audit logs. Claude Code and Claude for Microsoft 365 are also described as entering early access through the same environment. The applied-work signal is the combination of generative-AI workflows with administrative, compliance, spending, identity, and oversight controls required by public-sector organizations.

model_visible.headline: Introducing skills in the Gemini app and Workspace, plus what’s next for Gems
model_visible.excerpt: Google Workspace announced that reusable Gemini skills are moving into the Gemini app and Workspace and will eventually replace Gems for task-specific instruction sets. Google describes skills as reusable custom instructions that can be applied whenever a user prompts Gemini, allowing teams or individuals to avoid rebuilding the same directions for recurring work. The announcement gives rollout dates for Workspace and the Gemini app and explains that existing Gems will remain available during a transition before later migration. The broader Skills implementation is based on a portable Markdown-native skill pattern, which makes the concept useful beyond a single one-off chat. For the Brief, this is the one reusable Agent Skills story: encode a repeatable procedure once, maintain it, and reuse it.

model_visible.headline: Agents you can coach: how Asana builds human-agent teams with Claude
model_visible.excerpt: Anthropic’s Asana case study describes AI teammates that operate in the same work graph as human collaborators, with explicit roles, visible tasks, scoped access, pre-built skills, integrations, and shared memory. Each agent has a profile showing its purpose, allowed users, administrators, instructions, skills, integrations, and permissions. Asana says effective agent access is bounded by the permissions of the person who triggers it. Shared memory is separately governed: anyone can give task feedback, but only administrators and editors can commit changes to permanent memory or undo them. The operating model separates people who use an agent from the smaller set of subject-matter experts who govern its durable behavior.

model_visible.headline: Building an AI-powered contract intelligence platform with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
model_visible.excerpt: AWS presents a contract-intelligence reference architecture for organizations managing large portfolios of vendor contracts. Contract PDFs enter an automated pipeline where one agent extracts structured fields and a separate model independently verifies them. When the two disagree about signature detection, Amazon Textract supplies a deterministic tiebreaker. Verified results are stored in PostgreSQL and exposed through dashboards plus natural-language queries in Amazon Quick, supporting both portfolio-wide aggregation and document-specific questions. The design uses AgentCore runtime for managed agent hosting and policy controls outside the agent code. The useful nontechnical pattern is a multi-step agent workflow with visible processing status, independent verification, structured storage, and a human-facing interface for questions.
